blocks.text: A ladder slides down a wall while its foot kicks out along the floor, and a wheel rolls down a ramp: in both, no point of the body moves in a circle about a fixed pin. Yet at any instant each body is turning about one definite point that you can find with a ruler by drawing two perpendiculars.

blocks.markdown: For a body in plane motion that is not translating, there is a unique point with zero velocity at that instant: the **instantaneous centre of rotation** (IC). The velocity of any point $P$ on the body is perpendicular to the line from the IC to $P$, and its magnitude is $v_P=\omega\,r_{P/IC}$, where $\omega$ is the angular velocity (rad/s) and $r_{P/IC}$ is the distance from the IC in m.

blocks.title: Locating the IC
blocks.text: Draw the velocity direction at two points $A$ and $B$ on the body. Draw a line through each point perpendicular to its velocity. These two lines meet at the IC. Its position can lie outside the body, and it changes with time.

blocks.caption: The angular velocity follows from any one known point speed and its distance to the IC.

blocks.title: Sliding ladder
blocks.prompt: A 4 m ladder leans against a smooth wall. Its foot $A$ slides away from the wall at 1.2 m/s when the ladder makes $60^\circ$ with the floor. Find the angular velocity of the ladder and the speed of the top $B$.

steps.text: Geometry: foot is $4\cos60^\circ=2.0$ m from the wall; top is $4\sin60^\circ=3.464$ m above the floor.

$A$ moves horizontally, so the perpendicular through $A$ is vertical. $B$ moves vertically, so the perpendicular through $B$ is horizontal. They meet at the point 2.0 m from the wall and 3.464 m above the floor. So $r_{A/IC}=3.464$ m and $r_{B/IC}=2.0$ m.

blocks.answer: $\omega=0.346$ rad/s and $v_B=0.693$ m/s. The IC is at the corner of the rectangle formed by the ladder's end positions.

blocks.markdown: **Special cases.** (a) If the velocities at $A$ and $B$ are parallel and equal, the perpendiculars are parallel and never meet: the IC is at infinity, $\omega=0$ and the body is in instantaneous translation. (b) If the velocities are parallel but different in magnitude, the perpendiculars are parallel but the IC lies on the common line through $A$ and $B$: it is where the line joining the velocity arrow tips meets that line (the velocities vary linearly with distance from the IC). (c) For a wheel rolling without slip, the IC is the contact point with the ground.

blocks.title: Rolling wheel
blocks.prompt: A wheel of radius 0.35 m rolls without slipping with its centre moving at 7 m/s. Find the speed of the top of the rim and of the rim point level with the centre.

steps.text: IC at the contact point, so the centre is $R=0.35$ m from the IC.
Top point is $2R=0.70$ m from the IC.
Point level with the centre is $\sqrt2R=0.495$ m from the IC.

blocks.answer: $v_{\text{top}}=14$ m/s (twice the centre speed) and $9.90$ m/s for the side point, directed perpendicular to its line to the contact point.

rows: Corner of rectangle formed by the perpendiculars
blocks.caption: Where the IC lies.

blocks.markdown: **Zero velocity, non-zero acceleration.** The IC is a point of zero velocity only **at an instant**. A moment later a different material point of the body is at rest, and the IC point has moved. The material point that happens to be at the IC has a velocity that is changing, so it has non-zero acceleration. For a wheel rolling at constant centre speed $v$, the contact point's acceleration is $a=\omega^2R=v^2/R$ directed toward the wheel centre (upward), not zero. For this reason $a_P=\alpha r_{P/IC}$ and $\omega^2 r_{P/IC}$ must **not** be used as if the IC were a fixed pivot.

blocks.caption: For rolling at constant speed $\mathbf a_G=0$, $\alpha=0$ and $\mathbf r_{IC/G}=-R\hat j$, giving $\mathbf a_{IC}=+\omega^2R\,\hat j$.

blocks.title: What the IC can and cannot do
blocks.text: Use the IC for **velocities** of all points of the body in one step. Use the relative-acceleration equation for **accelerations**, because the IC itself accelerates.

blocks.title: Common errors
blocks.text: Drawing the lines along the velocities instead of perpendicular to them, using the wrong distance (to the IC, not to a pin that may be far away), and claiming the IC has zero acceleration.

points: The IC is where the perpendiculars to two velocity directions meet; $v_P=\omega r_{P/IC}$.
Parallel equal velocities mean translation (IC at infinity); rolling without slip puts the IC at the contact point.
The IC has zero velocity but generally non-zero acceleration (for a rolling wheel, $\omega^2R$ toward the centre).

questions.stem: How is the instantaneous centre of a body located from the velocity directions of two of its points?

options.text: At the intersection of the lines drawn through each point perpendicular to its velocity
At the intersection of the lines along the two velocities
At the midpoint of the line joining the two points
At the centre of mass of the body

questions.correctOptionText: At the intersection of the lines drawn through each point perpendicular to its velocity

distractorRationale.b: The velocity of a point is perpendicular to its line from the IC, so these lines are not the right ones.
distractorRationale.c: The IC depends on the velocity directions, not on the midpoint.
distractorRationale.d: The IC is generally unrelated to the centre of mass.

questions.explanation: Each point moves perpendicular to its line to the IC, so the IC lies on the perpendicular through that point. Two such lines intersect at the IC.

questions.stem: A wheel of radius 0.30 m rolls without slipping on a flat road with its centre moving at 6 m/s. Find the speed of the highest point of the rim in m/s.
questions.explanation: The IC is the contact point, so the top point is $2R=0.60$ m from the IC while the centre is $R=0.30$ m. Therefore $v_{\text{top}}=2v_G=12$ m/s.

questions.stem: Two points $A$ and $B$ on a rigid body have velocities that are parallel, equal in magnitude and in the same direction. Where is the instantaneous centre?

options.text: At infinity, so the body is in instantaneous translation
At the intersection of the velocities

questions.correctOptionText: At infinity, so the body is in instantaneous translation

distractorRationale.a: That would give opposite velocities at $A$ and $B$.
distractorRationale.c: That would make $A$ stationary, not moving.
distractorRationale.d: The velocities are parallel and do not meet.

questions.explanation: Perpendiculars to parallel velocities are parallel and never meet, so the IC is at infinity. All points move with the same velocity and $\omega=0$.

questions.stem: A 5 m ladder slides with its top $B$ against a vertical wall and its foot $A$ on the floor. At the instant when the foot is 3 m from the wall (so the top is 4 m up), the top is sliding down at 2 m/s. Using the instantaneous centre, find the speed of the foot in m/s.
questions.explanation: The IC is at 3 m from the wall and 4 m above the floor. The top is 3 m from the IC, so $\omega=2/3=0.667$ rad/s. The foot is 4 m from the IC, so $v_A=0.667(4)=2.67$ m/s.

questions.stem: A connecting link has its instantaneous centre located. Point $A$ is 0.50 m from the IC and moves at 3.0 m/s, and point $B$ is 0.80 m from the IC. Find the speed of $B$ in m/s.
questions.explanation: The angular velocity is $\omega=v_A/r_A=3.0/0.50=6.0$ rad/s. Then $v_B=\omega r_B=6.0(0.80)=4.8$ m/s, perpendicular to the line from the IC to $B$.

questions.stem: A wheel rolls without slipping at constant centre speed along a road. Which statement about the point of the wheel at the instantaneous centre (contact point) is correct?

options.text: Its velocity is zero but its acceleration is $\omega^2R$ directed toward the wheel centre
Its velocity and acceleration are both zero
Its velocity is $v$ forward and its acceleration is zero
Its velocity is zero and its acceleration is $R\alpha$ forward

questions.correctOptionText: Its velocity is zero but its acceleration is $\omega^2R$ directed toward the wheel centre

distractorRationale.b: The contact point accelerates toward the centre because its velocity changes direction a moment later.
distractorRationale.c: The contact point is at rest relative to the ground.
distractorRationale.d: At constant speed $\alpha=0$, and the acceleration is centripetal, not tangential.

questions.explanation: The contact point has $\mathbf v=0$ but the relative acceleration equation gives $\mathbf a=\mathbf a_G+\boldsymbol\alpha\times\mathbf r-\omega^2\mathbf r=\omega^2R$ toward the centre. A point that is at rest at an instant need not be at rest a moment later.

questions.stem: A wheel of radius 0.25 m rolls without slipping at a constant 5 m/s. Find the magnitude of the acceleration, in m/s$^2$, of the material point of the rim that is at the instantaneous centre at the instant considered.
questions.explanation: The angular velocity is $\omega=v/R=20$ rad/s. The centre has no acceleration and $\alpha=0$, so the contact point has $a=\omega^2R=400(0.25)=100$ m/s$^2$ toward the centre.

questions.stem: A wheel of radius 0.30 m spins at 30 rad/s but its centre moves forward at only 6 m/s (the wheel is skidding). Where is its instantaneous centre?

options.text: At the ground contact point, 0.30 m below the centre
0.20 m directly below the centre, i.e. 0.10 m above the ground

questions.correctOptionText: 0.20 m directly below the centre, i.e. 0.10 m above the ground

distractorRationale.a: This would require rolling without slip with $v=R\omega=9$ m/s.
distractorRationale.b: A forward-moving centre with clockwise spin has its zero-velocity point below the centre.
distractorRationale.d: The wheel is rotating, so $\omega\ne0$ and the IC is at a finite distance.

questions.explanation: The IC lies below the centre at distance $d=v_G/\omega=6/30=0.20$ m, which is less than $R=0.30$ m, so it is above the ground. Rolling without slip would put it at $d=R$.

questions.stem: Describe how to find the instantaneous centre of a link from the velocity directions of two points on it, and explain what happens in the special case where the two velocities are parallel (a) equal and (b) unequal in magnitude.
markingGuide: Draw perpendiculars to the velocities at the two points
The intersection is the IC, with velocity directions then perpendicular to lines from it
Then $\omega=v/r$ and speeds of other points follow from $v=\omega r$
(a) parallel equal velocities: IC at infinity, instantaneous translation, $\omega=0$
(b) parallel unequal: IC lies on the line through the points where the line joining the velocity tips meets it
questions.explanation: The IC exists as a finite point whenever the body rotates. In case (b) the perpendiculars coincide, so a second construction using the linear variation of speed with distance is needed.

questions.stem: Explain why the instantaneous centre of a body has zero velocity but generally non-zero acceleration, using the rolling wheel as an example, and say what mistake this prevents.
markingGuide: IC is zero-velocity point only at the instant; the IC moves and the material point there changes
The material point at the IC has changing velocity, so non-zero acceleration
For rolling at constant speed, $\mathbf a_{IC}=\omega^2R$ toward the wheel centre (upward), from $\mathbf a_G=0$, $\alpha=0$
Shows how the relative-acceleration equation gives this
Warns against using the IC as a fixed pivot for accelerations: $a\ne\alpha r$ or $\omega^2r$ from the IC; use relative acceleration instead
questions.explanation: In steady rolling the contact point leaves the ground and rises vertically with zero initial speed, which is a cusp in its path; the vertical acceleration $\omega^2R$ is what turns it upward.
